title-group.article-title: Physiologically Based Pharmacokinetic Modeling of Valemetostat to Inform Dose Recommendations When Coadministered With CYP3A/P‐gp Modulators

abstract.title: ABSTRACT
abstract.p: Valemetostat tosylate (valemetostat) is an oral, potent, selective dual inhibitor of enhancer of zeste homolog (EZH)2 and EZH1, approved in Japan for the treatment of relapsed/refractory adult T‐cell leukemia/lymphoma and peripheral T‐cell lymphoma. Results from in vitro and clinical studies suggest that valemetostat is pre‐systemically metabolized by cytochrome P450 3A (CYP3A) in the gut and excreted into bile and urine via P‐glycoprotein (P‐gp) in its unchanged form and as an oxidative metabolite. In this study, a physiologically based pharmacokinetic (PBPK) model was developed by utilizing available in vitro and clinical pharmacokinetics (PK) data to predict the impact of CYP3A and P‐gp modulators on the PK of valemetostat. The developed PBPK model was validated against clinical drug–drug interaction studies with a moderate CYP3A inhibitor (fluconazole), a strong CYP3A/P‐gp dual inhibitor (itraconazole), and a strong CYP3A/P‐gp dual inducer (rifampicin), indicating that the contributions of CYP3A and P‐gp in the gut and liver to valemetostat PK were appropriately described in the PBPK model. The validated model was applied to assess the effect of either a CYP3A or a P‐gp inhibitor, or a moderate CYP3A inducer on valemetostat PK. The PBPK model incorporating the contribution of CYP3A and P‐gp in the gut and liver effectively estimated the effect of CYP3A/P‐gp modulators on valemetostat PK and can be used to inform dose recommendations for valemetostat upon coadministration with other treatments.

list-item.p:
What is the current knowledge on the topic? ○
Valemetostat is a CYP3A and P‐gp substrate, and previous DDIs trials demonstrated an increase in mean valemetostat Cmax and AUCinf upon coadministration with fluconazole (a moderate CYP3A inhibitor) or itraconazole (a strong CYP3A/P‐gp dual inhibitor) and a decrease with rifampicin (a strong CYP3A/P‐gp dual inducer), respectively.

What question did this study address? ○
Is valemetostat PK affected when CYP3A alone or P‐gp alone is inhibited, or when coadministered with a moderate CYP3A inducer? Can the developed PBPK model explain the contribution of CYP3A and P‐gp in the gut and liver on valemetostat PK?

What does this study add to our knowledge? ○
This study revealed the efficiency of PBPK modeling to assess DDI risks and estimate changes in valemetostat PK upon coadministration with CYP3A/P‐gp modulators in scenarios when they remain untested clinically.

How might this change clinical pharmacology or translational science? ○
PBPK modeling of valemetostat integrates in vitro and clinical data to facilitate the mechanistic understanding of PK. PBPK modeling can inform dose recommendations for valemetostat when coadministered with CYP3A/P‐gp modulators, without dedicated clinical DDI studies.

sec.title: Introduction
sec.p: Valemetostat tosylate (valemetostat) is a novel, potent, and selective dual inhibitor of enhancer of zeste homolog (EZH)2 and EZH1, currently under development for the treatment of various types of cancer, including non‐Hodgkin lymphomas (NHLs) and solid tumors [1, 2, 3, 4].

In clinical trials, valemetostat has shown encouraging antitumor response in patients with T‐cell and B‐cell NHLs [2, 3, 5]. Valemetostat is approved in Japan for the treatment of relapsed/refractory (R/R) adult T‐cell leukemia/lymphoma (ATLL) and R/R peripheral T‐cell lymphoma (PTCL) [6]. A daily dose of valemetostat 200 mg for the treatment of patients with R/R ATLL was demonstrated through exposure–response analyses to reach exposure ranges that provide satisfactory efficacy with acceptable safety [7].

The pharmacokinetics (PK) of valemetostat have been studied in healthy individuals and in patients with R/R NHL. Maximum plasma concentration (Cmax) and area under the concentration–time curve (AUC) of valemetostat increased in a dose‐proportional manner in healthy participants who received single oral doses ranging from 50 to 200 mg under fasting conditions [8]. The mean Cmax and median time to Cmax (Tmax) for a 200 mg dose were ∼1500 ng/mL and 4.5 h, respectively. After reaching Cmax, valemetostat plasma concentrations declined with a mean apparent terminal elimination half‐life (t1/2) of ∼20 h. Valemetostat exposures were generally higher in patients with NHL compared with healthy participants, and the difference could be explained by plasma protein binding (PPB), mainly to alpha‐1 acid glycoprotein (AAG) [2, 9].

In vitro studies have demonstrated that valemetostat is a substrate of cytochrome P450 3A (CYP3A) and P‐glycoprotein (P‐gp) (Sections 1, 2). In a phase 1 drug–drug interaction (DDI) study of 32 healthy Japanese adult males, Cmax and AUC extrapolated to infinity (AUCinf) of valemetostat (25 mg single dose) were ∼2.9‐ and ∼4.2‐fold higher, respectively, when coadministered with itraconazole (a strong CYP3A/P‐gp dual inhibitor), or ∼1.6‐fold higher for both parameters when coadministered with fluconazole (a moderate CYP3A inhibitor), compared with valemetostat alone [10]. Another phase 1 DDI study of valemetostat (200 mg) and rifampicin (a strong CYP3A/P‐gp dual inducer) in healthy Japanese participants showed that Cmax and AUCinf of total valemetostat decreased by ∼60% and ∼70%, respectively, when valemetostat was coadministered with rifampicin, compared with valemetostat alone [11]. These data suggest that CYP3A and P‐gp are involved in the metabolism of valemetostat and can alter its PK profiles in humans. Understanding clinically relevant DDIs for agents used in cancer treatment is very important, as multiple supportive therapies may be needed to treat the constellation of symptoms that accompany the disease [12, 13]. Specifically, antifungal and antimicrobial medications including itraconazole, fluconazole, and rifampicin are often part of the treatment regimen due to the high susceptibility of patients with cancer to fungal and bacterial infections [14, 15].

Physiologically based pharmacokinetic (PBPK) modeling has become an increasingly valuable tool to fill information gaps in the drug development process. PBPK modeling integrates available physicochemical, preclinical, and clinical data to predict drug PK and DDIs, particularly when clinical testing is not feasible [16, 17, 18, 19, 20, 21]. Between 2008 and 2017, 60% of investigational new drugs and new drug applications submitted to the US Food and Drug Administration included PBPK modeling for the prediction of enzyme‐based DDIs and 7% of transporter‐based DDIs [16]. As PBPK modeling outcomes are also well accepted by regulatory agencies in Europe (European Medicines Agency) and Japan (Pharmaceuticals and Medical Devices Agency), PBPK models may often represent viable alternatives to supporting DDI studies [19, 21]. Notably, PBPK modeling has demonstrated good performance for predicting the effect of CYP3A inhibition on the PK of CYP3A drug substrates [20].

The PBPK model presented in this article was developed by utilizing available in vitro and clinical PK data, and was used to analyze the impact of CYP3A and P‐gp modulators on valemetostat PK, particularly when CYP3A alone or P‐gp alone is inhibited, and when a moderate CYP3A inducer is coadministered.

sec.title: Valemetostat PBPK Model Development
sec.p: The PBPK model for valemetostat was developed using the Simcyp simulator version 19 (Certara Inc., Sheffield, UK). Table 1 presents the modeling strategy and the clinical study datasets used for model development, validation, and application. The default population profile of Sim‐Japanese was used for the simulation. For supporting data describing model development, validation, and application, see Figures S1–S6 and Tables S1–S9.

sec.title: Absorption
sec.p: Valemetostat absorption was described using a mechanistic model (Simcyp Advanced Dissolution Absorption and Metabolism [ADAM] model). The solubility of valemetostat in aqueous media is high and pH‐independent; therefore, “solution” was selected as the formulation in the ADAM model.

Membrane permeability and P‐gp‐mediated concentration‐dependent transport of valemetostat were estimated by the 3‐compartment model using the Simcyp In Vitro Data Analysis toolkit, version 4. These simulations used the apparent permeability coefficient (Papp) of valemetostat obtained in the presence of P‐gp inhibitor in Caco‐2 cell monolayer assays. More information, including the results of the valemetostat in vitro membrane permeability assay and the optimized P‐gp kinetic parameters, are presented in Table S1,S2.

sec.title: PPB and Distribution
sec.p: Valemetostat binds mainly AAG, as demonstrated in an in vitro PPB study. The mean in vivo fraction unbound (fu) in plasma at each time point (0.0548) assessed after administration of 200 mg valemetostat in the clinical study DS3201‐A‐J107 (“J107”; JapicCTI‐205,338) [11] was used in the PBPK model.
Valemetostat blood‐to‐plasma concentration ratio was 0.6, demonstrating no preferential partitioning into red blood cells.

Using physicochemical and PPB parameters and after reducing the tissue–plasma partition coefficient (Kp) of muscle (a large organ without clearance pathways of valemetostat) to 0.295, to recover Cmax after single oral dosing of valemetostat, the volume of distribution at steady state (VSS) was estimated to be 0.262 L/kg.

sec.title: Disposition and Elimination
sec.p: Renal clearance (CLR) was calculated based on AUCinf values after administration of 200 mg valemetostat in the fasted state in the clinical study DS3201‐A‐J103 (J103) [8] and the urinary excretion of unchanged valemetostat (10% of dose) after a single oral administration of 200 mg valemetostat in the mass balance study DS3201‐A‐U105 (U105) [22].

In an in vitro study using recombinant human CYP (rhCYP) isoforms, valemetostat was metabolized mainly by CYP3A4/5. Intrinsic clearance (CLint) values were calculated using the metabolic clearance after incubation of [14C]valemetostat with rhCYP isoforms (Table S3). The predicted valemetostat fu in an in vitro microsomal preparation (fumic) was 0.8089 (Simcyp version 19). The estimated values of CLint by CYP3A4 (13.9 μL/min/mg protein) and CYP3A5 (3.51 μL/min/mg protein) were used as initial inputs into the model.

The additional human liver microsomes CLint was calculated by adding the estimated CLint by other CYP isoforms (0.908 μL/min/mg protein) to the estimated CLint for glucose conjugation (0.668 μL/min/mg protein) obtained from the mass balance study (U105). The excretion rate of glucuronide (1.75%) and the AUC (13,600 ng·h/mL) in the mass balance study were used to calculate the CL of glucuronide in vivo. The CLint per human liver microsomes was then back‐calculated using data on microsome content in human liver, etc.

sec.title: Intestinal Free Drug Concentration and Availability
sec.p: Given the absence of information regarding the active uptake of valemetostat by the enterocyte, the fu in the gut (fugut) was set at a default value of 1.

The clinical study DS3201‐A‐J104 (J104) showed that the observed AUCinf and Cmax ratios with fluconazole were 1.58 and 1.61, respectively, and no change in plasma t1/2 was observed, suggesting that inhibition of the first‐pass metabolism by fluconazole is the major mechanism of DDI and the contribution of CYP3A metabolism to the systemic clearance of valemetostat is low [10]. Based on the 1.6‐fold increase in both AUCinf and Cmax of valemetostat, intestinal availability (FG) was considered to be < 0.625. To recover the low FG despite the low systemic clearance by CYP3A, a basolateral permeability scalar (BPS) was included in the PBPK model to adjust the rate of the drug leaving the enterocyte via the basolateral side of the enterocyte and entering the portal vein. The BPS for valemetostat was optimized to 0.01. A value < 1 leads to higher enterocyte exposure to the drug and to greater first‐pass extraction in the gut.

sec.title: Model Validation
sec.p: The optimized PBPK model was validated against clinical studies J103, J104, and J107. The study outcomes were used to verify the predicted PK profiles/exposures of valemetostat [8]. From the J104 study, the DDI of valemetostat with fluconazole was used to optimize the initial PBPK model, and the DDI with itraconazole was used to verify the final model. In the J104 study, participants received two single doses of 25 mg valemetostat: first alone on day 1, and then on day 11 or day 12 after repeated dosing with itraconazole (200 mg twice on day 6 followed by 200 mg once daily [QD] until day 20) or fluconazole (400 mg once on day 6 followed by 200 mg QD until day 21), respectively.

The J107 DDI study was used to verify potential valemetostat DDI with concurrent rifampicin. Conversely to CYP3A inhibitors, concomitant administration of repeated doses of rifampicin (600 mg QD for 15 days) reduced valemetostat exposure (200 mg single dose on day 9 of rifampicin dosing).

The PBPK model was validated by simulating 10 virtual trials of identical design, participant numbers, and baseline characteristics, to the clinical studies and comparing results with the data from clinical trials. The input parameters for fluconazole, itraconazole, and rifampicin can be found in Table S5a–c. In summary, the default compound library file for fluconazole was used, while the compound library files of itraconazole and OH‐itraconazole were modified by including the competitive inhibition constant (Ki) values for intestinal and hepatic P‐gp. The reported in vivo Ki value (0.0135 μM) was used as the intestinal Ki value of itraconazole [12]. For in vivo Ki values for hepatic P‐gp, the lowest values of the reported in vitro Ki values of itraconazole (0.048 μM) and OH‐itraconazole (0.49 μM) were incorporated in the respective compound files. In the simulations using the modified itraconazole model with P‐gp inhibition parameters, the effect of P‐gp inhibition on renal tubular secretion was taken into consideration (details in the Section 9), as itraconazole has been reported to reduce CLR of digoxin (a P‐gp substrate) [23]. In the simulation of DDI with itraconazole, the CLR of valemetostat was reduced to 1.15 L/h from 1.88 L/h in the model of valemetostat, assuming that itraconazole inhibits tubular secretion of valemetostat by 50%. The default compound parameter file for rifampicin was used, except for the maximal fold induction (Indmax) of CYP3A, which was adjusted from 16 to 8 to recover the effect of rifampicin on the PK of simvastatin, a high‐clearance, low‐FG drug metabolized by CYP3A. Additional details are described in Tables S6–S8. To evaluate the effect of induction of intestinal P‐gp by rifampicin, the transporter‐mediated intrinsic clearance for intestinal P‐gp (CLint,T) of valemetostat was increased by 3.5‐fold [24, 25].

sec.title: Model Application for Valemetostat as a Victim
sec.p: The validated PBPK model was used to simulate the effects of CYP3A and P‐gp modulators on valemetostat PK parameters and compare these outcomes with the observed values. All simulations were conducted using a therapeutic dose of 200 mg valemetostat, in sets of 10 virtual trials, each including 10 healthy participants (7 males and 3 females) aged 20 to 45 years.

Victim DDI predictions in the presence and absence of itraconazole as a strong CYP3A inhibitor (excluding the P‐gp inhibitory activity) or as a strong CYP3A/P‐gp dual inhibitor were obtained using the default and the modified library files of itraconazole and OH‐itraconazole, respectively. The effect of repeated doses of itraconazole (200 mg twice on day 1 and 200 mg QD on days 2–10) on a single oral dose of valemetostat (200 mg) on day 6 was simulated.

Victim DDI predictions in the presence and absence of the P‐gp inhibitor quinidine were conducted using the default library file of quinidine (Tables S5d–S5e). Simulations of valemetostat PK after administration of a single oral dose of valemetostat (200 mg) on day 3 with concomitant administration of repeated doses of quinidine (600 mg QD on days 1–6) were conducted. Victim DDI prediction under the assumption of complete P‐gp inhibition was also conducted by turning off intestinal and hepatic P‐gp‐mediated transport and using the CLR value of 0.411, indicating complete inhibition of renal secretion clearance.

Finally, the effect of efavirenz (600 mg QD over 12 days) as a moderate CYP3A inducer on a single oral dose of valemetostat 200 mg on day 9 was simulated. The efavirenz Indmax was calibrated from 9.9 in the default compound file to 5.14, using the rifampicin Indmax of 8. Additional details are described in Table S5f.

sec.title: Model Development
sec.p: In the PBPK model with initial input parameters, the maximum rate of transporter‐mediated efflux (Jmax) for intestinal P‐gp was set to 0, assuming that intestinal P‐gp was saturated at 200 mg as the plasma exposure of valemetostat increased in proportion to dose from 100 mg to 200 mg (Figure S6, Table S9). The predicted mean AUCinf and Cmax following a single dose of 200 mg valemetostat were 0.981‐fold and 0.57‐fold the observed values (Figure S1). Due to the overprediction of the AUCinf ratio by preliminary DDI simulation with fluconazole, 20% of the CLint by CYP3A metabolism was assigned to biliary clearance to reduce fmCYP3A4/5. In addition, VSS was optimized by changing the Kp for muscle to better recover the observed Cmax. Further, intestinal P‐gp was introduced to the model and Jmax was optimized to be 0.75 pmol/min/cm2 to recover AUCinf observed after a single oral 25 mg dose of valemetostat. These optimizations led to the development of a PBPK model with comparable predicted versus observed PK outcomes for valemetostat both at 25 and 200 mg doses (Figure S2, Table S4). The predicted mean Cmax and AUCinf for valemetostat were within 2‐fold of the observed values. The resulting PBPK model also showed comparable predicted versus observed Cmax and AUCinf ratios of valemetostat with fluconazole (Table S3, Figures 1, S4).

sec.title: Model Validation
sec.p: The PBPK model validation was done by comparing the simulated and the observed plasma exposures following single valemetostat doses of 50, 100, and 200 mg in healthy individuals. The simulated PK profiles of valemetostat were comparable to the clinical data up to 24 h post dose, but were underestimated after 48 h post dose. The predicted Cmax and AUCinf values were within 2‐fold of the observed values (Table 4, Figure S3).

The impact of itraconazole or rifampicin on valemetostat PK was also simulated. Table 3 and Figures 1 and S5 present the predicted versus observed DDI outcomes in the presence and absence of itraconazole (as a strong CYP3A/P‐gp dual inhibitor) and rifampicin (as a strong CYP3A inducer). The predicted mean Cmax and AUCinf of valemetostat were within 2‐fold of the observed values, and the predicted Cmax and AUC ratios were within 1.25‐fold of the observed values, both in the presence and absence of either itraconazole or rifampicin. These results suggest that the model was validated for the purpose of evaluating the effect of CYP3A/P‐gp modifiers on valemetostat PK.

sec.title: Model Application
sec.p: The validated PBPK model was used to predict the effect of CYP3A/P‐gp modulators on the PK of a single 200 mg oral dose of valemetostat. The predicted Cmax and AUC ratios are shown in Table 5 and Figure 1. A 2.13‐fold increase in mean Cmax and a 2.67‐fold increase in mean AUCinf of valemetostat was predicted when taken concomitantly with itraconazole as a strong CYP3A inhibitor (excluding its P‐gp inhibitory activity), compared with valemetostat alone.

DDI with a strong CYP3A/P‐gp dual inhibitor was simulated using the modified itraconazole and OH‐itraconazole files that contained P‐gp inhibition parameters and considering the inhibitory effect of itraconazole on the renal tubular secretion of valemetostat. A 2.59‐fold and a 4.08‐fold increase in mean the Cmax and mean AUCinf of valemetostat, respectively, were predicted upon concomitant administration of itraconazole, compared with valemetostat alone.
Concomitant administration of valemetostat with the P‐gp inhibitor quinidine resulted in a 1.30‐fold increase and a 1.34‐fold increase in mean Cmax and AUCinf of valemetostat, respectively.

Assessment of the impact of complete inhibition of P‐gp on valemetostat PK, by turning off intestinal and hepatic P‐gp‐mediated transport in the model, and assuming that renal secretion of valemetostat was completely inhibited, found that the Cmax and AUCinf increased 1.59‐fold and 2.58‐fold, respectively.

sec.title: Discussion
sec.p: This PBPK modeling analysis demonstrated the DDI liability of valemetostat as a victim of interactions mediated by CYP3A and P‐gp. The PBPK model was validated by comparing predicted PK outcomes with PK parameters observed in clinical trials, and the resultant model was used to estimate the potential DDI of valemetostat with CYP3A and P‐gp modulators.

Clinical DDI studies previously conducted with fluconazole (a moderate CYP3A inhibitor), itraconazole (a strong CYP3A/P‐gp dual inhibitor), and rifampicin (a strong CYP3A inducer) evaluated the contribution of CYP3A and P‐gp to valemetostat PK.

In a DDI study by Tachibana et al., Cmax and AUC of valemetostat were increased by fluconazole to the same extent (1.61‐fold and 1.58‐fold, respectively), while t1/2 remained largely unchanged (21.7 h in the absence of fluconazole and 19.2 h in the presence of fluconazole) [8]. The DDI study of valemetostat and rifampicin demonstrated a small decrease in t1/2 (22.6 h and 18.3 h in the absence and presence of rifampicin, respectively), and 58.3% and 71.4% decreases in Cmax and AUC, respectively, in the presence of rifampicin [11]. Despite the inhibition (by fluconazole) or induction (by rifampicin) of hepatic CYP3A, the observed small changes in the t1/2 were probably due to the small contribution of hepatic CYP3A to the total clearance of valemetostat. Furthermore, the mass balance study in humans demonstrated that valemetostat is mainly eliminated in an unchanged form, which accounts for 64.9% and 10.0% of the administered dose in feces and urine, respectively, and only small amounts of metabolites were detected in excreta [22]. Based on these findings, it was suggested that valemetostat is pre‐systemically metabolized by CYP3A in the gut, and mainly excreted into bile and urine via P‐gp in its unchanged form. Therefore, CYP3A modulators are thought to mainly affect the metabolism of valemetostat in the gut. In addition, from the PK parameters obtained in healthy individuals after valemetostat dosing at 25, 50, 100, and 200 mg, nonlinearity of Cmax was observed up to 50 mg, but not at 100 mg or higher (Figure S6, Table S9). This indicates that P‐gp contributes to the intestinal absorption of valemetostat at lower doses, such as 25 mg, which was used in the clinical DDI studies with fluconazole and itraconazole [10]. However, the intestinal efflux mediated by P‐gp may become saturated at higher doses (e.g., 200 mg), as used in other clinical trials [8, 11, 22]. Therefore, to appropriately describe the PK characteristics of valemetostat, the contribution of CYP3A and P‐gp in both the gut and liver should be incorporated into the valemetostat PBPK model.

The final valemetostat PBPK model estimated the Cmax and AUCinf after a single oral dose of valemetostat, within an acceptable range, and can accurately reproduce DDIs with CYP3A/P‐gp modulators. Overall, the valemetostat PBPK model could be utilized prospectively to evaluate the impact of untested CYP3A/P‐gp modulators on valemetostat PK.

The validated valemetostat PBPK model was applied to predict the magnitude of DDIs with a strong CYP3A inhibitor without P‐gp inhibition, a strong CYP3A/P‐gp dual inhibitor, a P‐gp inhibitor without CYP3A inhibition, and a moderate CYP3A inducer after a single oral 200 mg dose of valemetostat as a victim.

The model predicted 2.13‐fold and 2.67‐fold increases in the Cmax and AUCinf ratios of valemetostat after coadministration with itraconazole used as a strong CYP3A inhibitor, suggesting that a strong CYP3A inhibitor highly affects valemetostat PK. The model estimated 2.59‐fold and 4.08‐fold increases in the Cmax and AUCinf of valemetostat, respectively, when a single oral dose of 200 mg valemetostat is coadministered with itraconazole, which acts as a dual inhibitor.

The PBPK model predicted a relatively mild effect of quinidine, a P‐gp inhibitor, on valemetostat PK, with an increase in Cmax and AUCinf of approximately 30%. Previous studies reported that quinidine reduced renal clearance of digoxin [26]; however, the relationship between this reduction in renal clearance and P‐gp inhibition by quinidine remains unclear. In the present study, the CLR of valemetostat remained unaltered during the assessment of DDI with quinidine. Quinidine may mainly inhibit P‐gp in the gut, and to a lesser extent the P‐gp–mediated biliary elimination pathway, as the plasma concentration of quinidine (predicted average free concentration in plasma: 0.26 μM) was insufficient to inhibit the hepatic P‐gp compared with the Ki value of P‐gp (0.64 μM). Since biliary excretion via P‐gp is considered the main elimination pathway of valemetostat, the PBPK model was used to evaluate the maximal impact of P‐gp inhibition on valemetostat PK. After a single oral 200mg dose of valemetostat, increases in Cmax and AUC values were predicted to be 1.59‐fold and 2.58‐fold when the intestinal and hepatic. P‐gp‐mediated transport was turned off and complete inhibition of renal secretion clearance was taken into consideration. This suggests that P‐gp significantly contributes to valemetostat PK, and potent P‐gp inhibitors may increase the plasma exposure of valemetostat in a manner similar to strong CYP3A inhibitors.

P‐gp is considered to be nearly saturated when 200 mg of valemetostat is administered. The assessment of the effect of the intestinal P‐gp Ki value of itraconazole on valemetostat PK showed that the impact of intestinal P‐gp inhibition is relatively larger at 25 mg than at 200 mg of valemetostat (Table S10). The effect of quinidine on P‐gp inhibition in the small intestine also had only a minor impact on the PK of valemetostat at 200 mg of valemetostat. The effect of quinidine on the PK of valemetostat was shown to be due to P‐gp inhibition in the liver and primarily CYP3A inhibition (Table S11).

The impact of efavirenz as a moderate CYP3A inducer was also predicted by the PBPK model. Similarly to rifampicin (a strong CYP3A inducer), which decreased the valemetostat AUC by 71.4% [11], coadministration of efavirenz decreased the Cmax and AUCinf of valemetostat by 33.4% and 42.5%, respectively. Based on these findings, it is therefore recommended to avoid concomitant use of moderate‐to‐strong CYP3A inducers in order to maintain valemetostat exposure at the therapeutic dose of 200 mg QD.

This PBPK analysis has some limitations. In clinical studies, valemetostat exhibited an atypical absorption profiles, with double peaks in its plasma concentration–time profile in a large number of participants. This PBPK model did not include a component for the description of double peaks, since the physiologic mechanism of this phenomenon is still unknownand may explain why the reproducibility of Cmax values was poorer compared with that of AUC values (2‐fold in Cmax and 1.5‐fold in AUC difference between the predicted and observed values). However, the valemetostat PBPK model reproduced well the Cmax and AUC ratios observed in the clinical DDI studies with CYP3A/P‐gp modulators, confirming the model's suitability for assessing the impact of CYP3A/P‐gp modulators on valemetostat PK.

The valemetostat PBPK model was built to represent high first‐pass metabolism in the gut, as expected from the clinical study results described above, by optimizing BPS to adjust the rate of the drug leaving the enterocyte on the basolateral side of the enterocyte and entering the portal vein. The phenomenon of the double peaks in the absorption process may indicate the retention of valemetostat in the enterocyte. The final PBPK model predicted mean fraction absorbed (fa) and FG to be 0.43 and 0.53, respectively, after a single oral dose (200 mg) of valemetostat. The appropriateness of the predicted fa and FG could not be confirmed because the PK data after intravenous dosing of valemetostat are not available. However, this PBPK model could accurately reproduce the impact of CYP3A/P‐gp modulators on valemetostat PK. Therefore, we believe that the PK characteristics of valemetostat were well described by the valemetostat PBPK model.

No clinical DDI data are available for external validation of the in vivo Ki value on the liver of itraconazole. A sensitivity analysis was performed to evaluate the effect of itraconazole on hepatic P‐gp. When the Ki value was changed by a factor of 10, the AUC and Cmax ratios changed slightly, but the variation was within ±20% (Figure S7).

To assess the effect of itraconazole on the renal clearance of valemetostat, a sensitivity analysis was performed. At a valemetostat dose of 25 mg, the CLsec reduction of 50% most accurately reproduced the measured data (Table S12). Therefore, it is considered appropriate to reduce renal secretion clearance by 50% when coadministering itraconazole.

Using the final model, we evaluated the contribution of CLR when 5 mg of valemetostat was administered intravenously. When CLR was set to 0 L/h, the total clearance (CLtot) decreased by approximately 36% and the AUC increased by approximately 56% compared with the base model (CLR = 1.88 L/h). The contribution of CLR to CLtot was estimated to be approximately 36%.

In conclusion, our PBPK model successfully described the contributions of CYP3A and P‐gp to valemetostat PK. The model assessed the effect of CYP3A‐ and P‐gp‐modulating agents on plasma exposure to valemetostat. Taken together with results from clinical trials, these results can be used to inform dose recommendations for valemetostat when coadministered with CYP3A/P‐gp modulators.
